item.title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
item.abstract: November 23, 2026 Science Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush Read the paper How using agent teams and formal verification can improve quantum algorithms for modelling fusion energy, chemistry and enzymes Quantum computers could soon solve problems beyond the reach of classical supercomputers. However, there is a catch: even when using the best quantum algorithms, some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support. In a new paper , we used teams of Gemini 4 agents to improve well-known quantum algorithms, creating highly efficient quantum circuits. These optimized circuits, which are instructions for how a quantum computer should carry out an algorithm, could one day help us run simulations that solve complex scientific challenges, from fusion energy to drug design. To help the community build on this work, we are open-sourcing our Lean library , problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub. Because we cannot test resource-intensive quantum circuits on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, we have to prove that they work mathematically. Our agent teams proved each result using Lean, a formal theorem prover. Your browser does not support the video tag. Improving quantum algorithms using agentic teams For each problem, we tasked separate, independent agent teams with finding algorithmic improvements. These ideas were then verified with Lean, before entering a shared notebook. Every four hours, agents from each team met at a virtual conference to trade, debate and compare ideas. As teams produced more effective ideas over time, the computational cost gradually fell until the experiment finished. We chose to focus on applications that could one day impact some of humanity’s greatest challenges, such as clean energy and drug design, but our method is not limited to these problem areas. We found a quantum circuit that helps calculate an important property of inertial confinement fusion, a fusion reaction method that uses lasers to compress hydrogen fuel until ignition. Our agent teams cut the required computing cost (a metric that combines required qubits and operations) by 11.8×, and lowered required memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits . The agents also reduced costs for simulating molecules in drug metabolism and certain photochemical reactions, which are complex reactions that are difficult for classical computers to simulate. For a common light-sensitive molecule, the agent teams made quantum simulation 8× cheaper, simplifying how the algorithm tracks particle positions and electric forces. For Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most human medicines and is important for drug design, they found a 2.5× improvement and lowered memory from 481 to 333 qubits, by replacing bulky memory lookups. We also improved a fundamental quantum algorithm and a widely used arithmetic building block. We found a 2.57x speedup for a specific implementation of Grover's algorithm, a foundational quantum operation that searches through an unsorted list, and a 290x speedup for arcsin, a common routine that is used by many other quantum algorithms to load numbers into quantum states. Running these algorithms in scientific simulations would still demand more computational resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide, but these improvements are significant. We are also excited by the way in which we found them. We built a new, open-source library , in Lean for quantum algorithms which could be used by teams of collaborating agents, so their ideas were backed by mathematical correctness guarantees. We could then set the research direction by specifying the problems for our agent teams and supervise their progress. Our knowledge of quantum algorithms, combined with the way we set up our agent teams, led to real scientific results. The same approach could also accelerate other aspects of quantum computing research, and scientific discovery more broadly. Proof-checked AI search compresses work that once took years of manual design, empowering researchers to focus on choosing problems and interpreting results. item.title: Z AI Releases GLM-5.4: A 750B Loop Transformer That Runs 28 Layers Twice
item.abstract: Z.ai has released GLM-5.4 , its first flagship model built on a Loop Transformer architecture. The GLM-5.4 Loop Transformer runs 28 layers of the GLM-5 base model for 2 iterations. Z.ai says the model reaches intelligence comparable to 2T-3T parameter models. For developers, the pitch is ‘Generalized Coding’: code as the tool for video, games, 3D shaders and CAD. GLM-5.4 is a 750B-scale Loop Transformer from Z.ai that runs shared layers twice per pass. It ships first inside Z.ai’s own products: the GLM Coding Plan , the ZCode desktop app and Z.ai Chat . Z.ai did not pre-train a looped model from scratch. It adapted the pre-trained GLM-5 base through continued training. The technical post states that looped models trained from scratch still trail unshared models at equal compute. Adapting an existing base raises the ceiling with a relatively small compute overhead. In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In GLM-5.4, a group of 28 weight-shared layers runs for 2 iterations. Z.ai made 3 changes to keep this practical at 750B scale. Overwriting hidden states across loops made activation norms blow up. GLM-5.4 adds independent per-token gates for each iteration. The first pass writes small updates and builds global context. The second pass opens the gates to refine the output. On harder tokens, the first pass writes more aggressively. A naive design keeps a full KV cache for every loop. GLM-5.4’s second loop reuses the sparse KV selected in pass 1. It keeps its own new KV only inside a local sliding window. So the extra loop costs 1 sliding window of KV cache, not a full context cache. Z.ai says this keeps the cost increase over GLM-5.3 under control at 1M context. The second loop reuses the indices from the first loop’s indexer. That adds zero indexing overhead. Z.ai reports near-identical results versus recomputing indices on every pass. Z.ai has not published benchmark scores for the 750B GLM-5.4 model. A Z.ai team member said scores will come later, per DataCamp . The evidence in the blog is an iso-parameter ablation on a 30B model. It shares the 750B base’s architecture. The looped version used about 10% more total training compute. Scores were measured after 200K long-context SFT with thinking mode on. Source: Z.ai GLM-5.4 blog . Self-reported, 30B model, not the 750B flagship. Two patterns stand out. The largest gains come in math, science reasoning and long context. Output length also falls on most tasks. MMLU-Pro answers got 14.9% shorter and GPQA-Diamond answers 11.7% shorter. Z.ai says part of the reasoning moves into the loop’s implicit depth. AIME25 is the exception: output length dropped only 2%. Z.ai validated the design on 1B, 4B, 30B and 750B bases. The ‘2T-3T parameter’ claim has no flagship table behind it yet. Z.ai calls this direction Generalized Coding. It credits gains in both coding and vision. The technical sections shows four demos: These are vendor demos, not benchmarks. Z.ai reports up to 200 tokens/s off-peak and 70-80 tokens/s at peak load. It fused core kernels to cut intermediate memory traffic. Access today runs through the GLM Coding Plan, ZCode and Z.ai Chat. ZCode is Z.ai’s desktop agent harness for GLM-5.4. It runs on macOS, Windows and Linux (Beta). The Coding Plan lists Lite at $12.6/month, Pro at $56 and Max at $117.6. Z.ai says prices may change. Check out the official GLM-5.4 tech blog and try it in ZCode . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.? item.title: The enterprise guide to securing coding agents
item.abstract: Shipping fast and secure Coding agents likely write code and open pull requests at your organization already. For many leading enterprises, they are reviewing, testing, and merging it too. For example, after standardizing on Claude Code across its engineering organization, Salesforce ¹ reported : 79% more pull requests merged per developer at Salesforce 5% fewer total incidents at Salesforce As agents do more, technical and security leaders must mitigate risks like prompt injection and privilege abuse with layered controls such as checked permissions and bounded environments. The first two chapters focus on scoping the risk. We discuss the requirements every AI provider should meet and four agentic risks to mitigate. The next three chapters focus on bounding the risk. We highlight the defensive layers you can deploy with Claude Code as well as how to centrally manage and enforce those controls. This guide aims to provide a helpful agent security framework that can give organizations the confidence and trust to run agents effectively at scale. The components of defending an AI agent: the model, the environment around it, and external checks on what goes in and what comes out. This guide is written for organizations on Claude Team and Enterprise plans. If you reach Claude through a cloud provider such as AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure, the same principles and local controls apply. 01 Setting the bar for agent security Six questions for every coding agent · Applying SaaS requirements to your AI provider “A CISO's responsibility in the age of agentic AI is not to achieve zero risk. Instead, our jobs are to make agentic risk legible and bounded. This way, we can deliberately accept what we can manage, so the business moves on our terms instead of around us.” Jason Clinton , Deputy CISO at Anthropic Six questions for every coding agent Here are six questions leaders can ask when evaluating coding agents to verify they are enterprise ready. Question to ask Why you should care Good answer Weak answer Does the model refuse when it should? The model is the first check on a harmful request, making a bad action less likely. Refusal trained into weights, with published rates. "Our system prompt instructs the model to decline." Are actions automatically inspected outside the model before they run? External checks can catch when the model is tricked or using bad judgment. Static analysis of commands and a separate evaluator model. Prompt injection probes. "The model is very capable." Is blast radius bounded by the environment? This bounds the severity, and therefore risk, of an incident. Kernel-level sandboxing that admins can require and set to fail closed, or an isolated VM for each session. Egress allowlisting at the network layer. "The agent is instructed not to leave the working directory." Can policy be locked centrally? Sets minimum standards that can’t be undone by individuals. Managed settings with hard-deny rules a local user can't override. “Per-developer config files, and an honor system policy doc.” Is the code the agent writes secure? Code volume is scaling and vulnerabilities can ship unless checks scale with the volume. Automated security review with a person approving high-risk changes. “The model is trained to write secure code.” Can you reconstruct an incident? Compliance. Improving security over time. Session telemetry export , audit API (Enterprise), and named known gaps. "Logs are available on request." Applying SaaS requirements to your AI provider You already have a SaaS provider checklist with controls such as single sign-on, role-based access, data handling terms, and audit logs. Hold AI providers to a similar checklist. For example, Claude Code supports these security expectations through: Single sign-on and role-based access control (Enterprise), managed the way you manage your other enterprise tools. We don’t train generative models on code or prompts under our commercial terms, unless your organization has chosen to share that data with us. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (rolling out in phases) combines the privacy of zero data retention with state-of-the-art safeguards for detecting misuse across highly capable models. Data can be encrypted with your own keys and kept in storage you control for a limited time. Learn more . On Enterprise, BAA coverage for the Claude Code CLI and the desktop app’s Code tab in local mode, once the HIPAA configuration is applied. Encryption options on cloud platforms: customer-managed keys in AWS KMS on Amazon Bedrock, CMEK on Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry’s Hosted on Azure option. A SOC 2 Type 2 report and ISO 27001 certificate in the Anthropic Trust Center . 02 Identifying AI-specific risks Leaked credentials and privilege abuse · Unvetted dependencies and extensions · Data exfiltration · Prompt injection Security and technical leaders are familiar with risks like leaked credentials, abused privileges, compromised dependencies, and insider threats. However the attack surfaces, velocity, and scale all change when it comes to agents. Let’s look at some of the risks. Risk How you handle it today What changes with an agent Leaked credentials and privilege abuse Least privilege, short-lived tokens, keyless auth through workload identity or OIDC. Regular review of over-privileged accounts. Named accounts for people, per-workload identity for software. Credentials should be short-lived and scoped to the task or job, not the developer’s full access. The agent acts inside a developer’s session and most logs outside Claude Code only show the developer’s name. Unvetted dependencies and extensions Pinned versions, review gates, two reviewers on manifest changes. Version controlled configuration. Agents add both vetted and unvetted dependencies faster than manual processes. Extensions instruct the agent the moment they connect. Data exfiltration Egress allowlisting at the network layer. A compromised agent can send data out through services you already allow. Unlike traditional malware, it can try multiple routes the attacker doesn’t have to proactively define. Insider risk Social engineering awareness training, verification, reporting paths. Prompt injection: The check moves to the tool call and the network boundary. Risk 1: Leaked credentials and privilege abuse Anything an agent can read, it can leak. That includes credentials like a long-lived AWS access key or GitHub token. Anything the agent can do, a compromised or overeager agent can misuse. By default, an agent in Claude Code runs under the identity of the developer who oversees it. In the event of an incident, you may need to distinguish between agent and developer actions so you can appropriately respond. Illustrative example of a pull request conversation. In the pipeline, the agent’s work arrives under its own name. Risk 2: Unvetted dependencies and extensions Agentic coding accelerates the rate at which code is generated and reviewed, which includes the speed at which dependencies are added and configuration changes are made. When you ask an agent to add JSON schema validation, it will find a package, add the latest version, and have working code in minutes. That speed can be a risk if agents aren’t pointed in the right direction. MCP servers, plugins, skills, subagent definitions, and a repository’s CLAUDE.md file are dependencies too, and they deserve the review you give a package. Unlike a compromised library, which waits to be called, they reach the agent as soon as they load. Their descriptions and instructions enter the context window before the agent has done any work. On Enterprise plans, skill and plugin scanning checks third-party skills and plugins for malicious content when someone uploads or edits them in your organization. Illustrative example of what an admin sees when skill and plugin scanning blocks a plugin on an Enterprise plan. Risk 3: Data exfiltration Every leak needs a route out.

item.title: 實測：1450億參數塞進筆記本，每秒狂飆80+Token！國產端側大模型殺瘋了
item.abstract: 實測：1450億參數塞進筆記本，每秒狂飆80+Token！國產端側大模型殺瘋了 思邈 2026-11-23 19:01:15 來源： 量子位 零Token成本，斷網也能自由Vibe Coding 允中 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號QbitAI 上個月，曾經風靡全球的AI陪伴平臺Character.AI，申請了破產保護。 資料顯示，其月活躍使用者數（MAU）一度高達2200萬。破產時，在公司披露的經營困境中，核心因素之一就是 算力成本 。 這就出現了一個悖論： AI產品越成功，有時候反而越會帶來巨額虧損。 那有沒有可能，讓更多AI能力直接在本地執行，而不必事事依賴雲端？ 這正是端側AI近年來持續探索的方向。 但想把大模型真正搬到手機、PC等終端，並沒有那麼簡單。受限於裝置的視訊記憶體、記憶體頻寬、儲存和功耗，模型規模越大，越需要解決如何載入、如何排程，以及如何保證實際推理速度的問題。 行業急迫需要端側模型的進步。以蘋果此前公佈的3B參數端側基礎模型為例，其主要面向內容生成、摘要、分類和多輪對話等任務。蘋果當時也曾表示，這款模型並非為處理世界知識類問題或高階推理任務而設計。 此時，破局者出現了。 無界方舟近日釋出了端側大模型 Edge0-145B ，總參數量達到1450億，官方將其稱為「全球首個千億參數端側原生基礎模型」。 開源僅上線3天，便衝上了 Hugging Face的Text Generation榜單TOP 1 。 同時，該模型還在海外平臺Today’s News頁面中位列首位。 這個模型厲害的地方在於， 它突破了端側模型行業的智慧上限，還能在PC或高配筆記型電腦上執行。 在官方釋出的介紹影片中，Edge0-145B可以斷網Vibe Coding手搓小遊戲，且推理速度在80+ token/s。 咱們先來看看端側模型在這兩年的規模演進圖，雖然端側模型的參數被不斷推高，從1B到30B，但幾乎都停留在理論階段，硬體帶動不了。 從圖中可以看到，無界方舟第一次將端側模型拔高到千億參數水平 ，145B斷崖式領先。他們宣傳的特色就是「模型真正可用，不是實驗室裡的Demo」。 根據評測結果，145B參數的端側模型，智力水平已經可以對標雲端模型Claude Opus 4.6、DeepSeek-V4-Flash、Qwen3.8-Flash-Next等知名模型。對於長期以輕量化、小參數模型為主的端側領域而言，這也提供了一種新的技術探索方向。 這就意味著，它是一個可以Vibe Coding的端側模型，全程可斷網使用、無token費用。 斷網真能Vibe Coding 接下來，測試團隊按照官方公佈的配置要求，選用一臺NVIDIA RTX Spark筆記本進行實測。 裝置要求上，Edge0-145B最低可在配備12GB視訊記憶體、20GB系統記憶體的PC上執行，也支援配備48GB統一記憶體的Mac。 不得不說，曾經如果想把145B的雲端模型做私有化部署，還需要裝配180-300萬元的伺服器，現在僅需要約1.5萬元的筆記本就能流暢帶動。 團隊實測了三個案例，分別考察它在3D建模、遊戲製作和影片生成上的表現。 他們不止實測了Edge0-145B，還與雲端模型做了對比，來看看端側模型是否真的可以實現“比肩雲端模型”。 他們選擇了主流雲端模型GPT-6 Astra和Claude Opus 4.8進行對比。（沒有選擇Fable的理由，一方面是燒錢燒心，另一方面是沒幾個雲端模型可以跟它對打。） 實測1：3D建模（紐約時代廣場） 給了一段相同的prompt，讓Edge0-145B和主流雲端模型GPT-6 Astra、Claude Opus 4.8分別生成一個紐約時代廣場的三維場景。 任務要求： 在Blender裡搭建紐約時代廣場（Times Square）的當代夜景3D場景，並渲染一段20秒的穿梭飛越影片。鏡頭會在兩側佈滿LED廣告屏的“峽谷”裡低空穿行，依次貼近掠過多個標誌性景點，每個景點都要經得起近看。 說實話Edge0-145B的生成效果遠超預期，看起來和GPT-6 Astra不相上下，且這兩者都遠遠好於Claude Opus 4.8。團隊起初甚至以為把模型名字寫反了…… 大部分場景下，Edge0-145B和GPT-6 Astra難分上下，霓虹屏、街谷和高樓視窗都清晰可見，光影氛圍真實。 整體上看，GPT-6 Astra的氛圍更明亮一些，而Edge0-145B生成的霓虹廣告牌效果明顯優於兩個雲端模型，有更多設計感和視覺差異化。 實測2：遊戲製作（中世紀教堂） 在RPG-3D遊戲開發場景，同樣的任務和prompt，團隊也用三個模型做了對照。 任務要求： 為一款奇幻RPG遊戲搭建一個原創的中世紀主城場景：一座哥特式大教堂和它前面的城市廣場。做成遊戲宣傳片級別的3D場景，並渲染一段20秒的飛越影片。鏡頭會從老城上空俯衝到廣場，穿過大教堂主門洞，一路飛到中殿盡頭，每個景點都要經得起近看。場景是原創的虛構城市，不要復刻任何現有遊戲或影視作品裡的場景。 三個模型一對比，Claude Opus 4.8在細節的刻畫上略有欠缺。再看Edge0-145B和GPT-6 Astra，二者的產出效果十分接近。 在石板廣場的噴泉設計上，GPT-6 Astra生成的畫面更為精緻；而在教堂牆面的結構與細節方面，以及殿堂內部的彩色玻璃窗和拱頂的畫面上，Edge0-145B生成的效果都更好。 這些效果是在筆記型電腦上斷網跑出來的，全程沒有消耗任何token費用。 實測3：影片生成（機械原理科普） 為了呈現酷炫的效果，團隊讓三個模型用一套機器視覺檢測系統，把一臺渦輪噴氣發動機按照進氣道、壓氣機、燃燒室、渦輪和噴管拆開，並拆解標註各部分的執行溫度和零件編號。 任務要求： 做一段15秒的豎版產品動效短片：一臺渦輪噴氣發動機（turbojet）被一套“機器視覺檢測系統”拆開檢查，各段沿發動機軸向依次爆炸分離，螢幕上疊加追蹤框和英文標註，高溫段被熱場著色，然後重新裝好，最後落成一張乾淨的白底產品圖，並且首尾無縫迴圈。 在零件溫度的呈現上，Edge0-145B的熱色帶是深紫→品紅→琥珀→近白，熱色集中在燃燒室、渦輪和尾噴管，壓氣機保持溫熱狀態，更符合真實情況；而右邊Opus 4.8的生成效果沒有可讀的熱場圖例，標註文字也堆疊在了一起。 過去，這需要硬體工程師和三維設計師接力數天才能完成；現在，一臺高配筆記本在一個多小時內就能獨立交付。 從實測結果來看，Edge0-145B在部分任務上的表現，已經非常接近GPT-6 Astra等雲端模型。 更重要的是，在滿足配置要求的筆記型電腦上，Edge0-145B可以實現本地離線執行。 這意味著，使用者可以減少對雲端API的依賴，降低token呼叫成本。 對於政企、醫療、金融等對資料安全和隱私保護要求較高的行業，本地部署也提供了另一種AI使用方式，有助於減少敏感資料上傳雲端帶來的安全與合規壓力。 對於硬體廠商而言，裝載端側模型後，也可以拓展更多離線、弱網場景下的應用空間，進一步開啟海外市場。 “高智力端側模型的開創者”到底是誰？ 國產大模型Edge0，來自於創立僅兩年半的“無界方舟AutoArk”。 創始人曾曉東博士是MIT TR35獲獎者，也曾經是螞蟻技術實驗室的聯合創始人，曾主導支付寶盒、刷臉支付、無人超市等專案。 聯合創始人小喬，是今年Forbes福布斯華人精英TOP100入選者，個人獲得過37個國際獎項，涉及產品、設計、業務等不同領域。 團隊成員來自位元組、阿里、螞蟻、Google、Tesla、斯坦福、清華、復旦等知名企業與院校。 早在今年9月初，無界方舟就推出了 全球第一個可以在手機上流暢執行的35B端側模型：Edge0-35B 。 據介紹，這是全球範圍內，首次能讓一個350億參數的模型流暢地跑在手機上 。峰值記憶體不到2.5GB，在iPhone 18 Pro Max上的生成速度超過37 token/s。外網釋出帖的閱讀量在當天就突破了120萬，來自OpenAI、NVIDIA、高通等公司的多位技術專家和研究員紛紛轉發，模型也曾登上Hugging Face全站Trending榜第一。 他們同時開源了模型權重和統一推理框架，成為了端側企業和研究機構復刻的標準解法。此後，行業對端側模型的討論，從“幾十億參數”抬升到了350億參數這一檔。 而Edge0-145B的開源，代表著無界方舟在“探索端側智慧上限”這條路上又邁出了一大步。 與釋出同步，Edge0-145B在Hugging Face開放模型權重，全新的端側統一推理引擎在GitHub開源，並提供一鍵部署工具與完整硬體適配指南。釋出首日Day 0即全面支援macOS、Windows、Linux三大系統，覆蓋蘋果M系列晶片，以及NVIDIA RTX Spark、RTX 4090 / 5090等GPU平臺。 從1450億參數的模型架構，到配套推理引擎、部署工具和硬體適配方案，無界方舟正在探索一條面向實際終端應用的高智力端側模型路線。 全新技術路線，為端側而生 先來看看端側行業這兩年是怎麼卷的，主流思路就一個字：小。 模型一大，硬體就帶不動，所以端側模型的發展路徑從7B、3B，一路壓到1B，來換取更低的記憶體和功耗。代價是，參數越小，模型越笨。 以手機為例，端側模型的規格大多停留在3B左右，此類模型只能處理一些文案改寫、訊息提煉等簡單任務。 蘋果把on-device寫成Apple Intelligence的基石，更複雜、需要更大算力的請求再走Private Cloud Compute；谷歌提供可“優先端側、不行再上雲”的Hybrid Inference；微軟則寫下：“最豐富的AI體驗，只有雲和裝置一起工作時才可能。” 所以端側模型幾乎很難存在“小而美”。要麼“小而笨”，要麼“大到得上雲端”。 市面上，非手機和車機廠商推出的端側模型，即使把參數做小，仍面臨實際應用方面的挑戰，多數還停留在demo階段。 端側模型要 真正可用 ，得同時滿足五個條件： 記憶體裝得下、首字等得起、生成跟得上、功耗壓得住、長任務不變慢。 Edge0-145B交出的成績是： 記憶體裝得下： 視訊記憶體12G+記憶體20G以上即可流暢執行，也支援配備48GB統一記憶體的Mac。一臺中高階的個人筆記本或桌上型電腦就能執行，不需要伺服器； 首字等得起： 預填充（Prefill）速度1,100+token/s，幾十頁程式碼丟進去，第一個字即時出現； 生成跟得上： 解碼（Decode）速度80+token/s，比人的閱讀速度更快，不用盯著螢幕一個詞一個詞地等； 功耗壓得住： 典型功耗約80W，持續執行不降頻； 長任務不變慢： 支援128K–256K上下文，長文本下速度基本不衰減，長時間的複雜任務不會越跑越慢。 Edge0-145B的官網詳情頁，放了一張詳細的速度表： 以RTX 5090 D 24GB為例，NVFP4版本，智慧體解碼98.3 token/s，16K預填充3165.7 token/s；Q3_K版本更快一些，分別是121.2 token/s和3554.9 token/s。 Edge0-145B可以在滿足配置要求的筆記型電腦上流暢執行；Edge0-35B可以在手機上高速跑動。 這背後，無界方舟走了一條完全不同的技術路線：做 端側的原生基礎模型，且模型與推理框架協同設計與最佳化 ，而不是把雲端模型壓小。 關鍵在於， 它每次只調動其中一小部分參數。 據官網介紹，Edge0-145B採用 全新的潛空間稀疏MoE（Latent MoE）架構 ，把48層裡的專家全部重做 。 原來專家在2560維的寬空間裡算，現在先壓進一個窄空間（145B用1792維，120B用1280維）算，算完再還原回去。 一個專家從一大塊權重，變成固定1.63 MB的一條記錄，專家總參數145B少30%。 因為結構改了，所以他們用大量的資料重新訓了一輪，而且是直接按4 bit訓出來的，沒有在訓練後再壓縮。 另外，模型還搭配了一個全新的推理引擎 ， 視訊記憶體、記憶體、硬碟三級分層放權重。常用的專家留在視訊記憶體裡，不常用的按需搬進來，再加上投機解碼（一次猜幾個token再驗證）和雙卡協同。 能力上，除了團隊上面的實測可證明“端側智力首次比肩雲端”以外，也可以看看官方公佈的測試結果。 其中最亮眼的，要數 智慧體和程式設計 方面。 Terminal-Bench 2.1上，Edge0-145B拿下86.5，高於Qwen3.8-Flash-Next的83.3、DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731的82.7，也高於Claude Opus 4.6（Max）的78.2。 DeepSWE 1.1上，它拿到64.6，高於Flash-Next的58.7和DeepSeek的54.4。 產業佈局，是端側AI壁壘 從模型佈局來看，無界方舟成立兩年多來，已推出200+模型，其中覆蓋了端側大語言模型、語音模型、決策模型、向量模型等不同領域，充分滿足產業落地場景。 模型參數從0.1B到145B，可適配從機器人、PC、手機、筆記型電腦等中高配置硬體，到AI耳機、AI眼鏡、AI玩具等低配置硬體，每一檔都有對應的端側模型。 合作客戶包含多家知名消費硬體廠商，比如聯想、韶音、奇多多星球等；也有晶片類企業，比如地瓜機器人、高通等；此外還有多家AI軟體企業。 截至2026年10月， 企業客戶數已超過11萬家，包含大量由開源社群使用者轉化而來的頭部KA客戶 。 無界方舟的技術與產業落地，已經形成“飛輪”效應。 端側市場高度碎片化，不同晶片的NPU架構不同，對INT4、INT8、FP4等計算精度的支援各不相同，通用模型直接部署很難發揮硬體效能。 無界方舟具備從模型到推理引擎的深度調優能力，已適配95%的主流晶片平臺，如高通、恆玄、瑞芯微、全志、地瓜等，合作產業也覆蓋了耳機、眼鏡、手機、PC、機器人等各類硬體賽道。 端側會替代雲端嗎？ 多年來，端側模型都是雲端模型的補充和輔助，大眾也已經把AI得上雲端當作理所應當。 但如果端側模型已經可以對標雲端模型的表現，可以完成Vibe Coding等任務，成為生活和工作中的生產力，雲端便不再是唯一的答案，AI開始擁有更多走進日常工作和生活的方式。 使用端側模型，最顯著的好處有兩點：AI普惠、資料合規。 首先，AI不再有高昂的token成本。以一名開發者Vibe Coding為例，每天8小時約消耗1,000萬token，每月按22個工作日計，一年可以省下5-10萬元支出。 以B端企業為例，雲端token成本每年高達數百萬到幾十億不等，端側AI可降低90%以上的成本。 在純雲方案裡，AI是一項隨銷量增長而增加的成本；在端側方案裡，它變成了一項隨銷量增長而獲得的利潤。 第二，使用者隱私和企業資料合規都將有保障。端側模型將所有資料閉環在本地硬體中，資料不再上雲。可以放心讓端側AI讀取發票、財報、訂單和客戶資料，資料本地化是AI能在商業場景深度應用的前提。 在使用者和產業的需求上，token成本普惠、隱私合規有保障、斷網弱網可用，這些雲端模型的痛點剛好是端側模型的先天優勢。 未來，雲和端的邊界在哪裡？ 無界方舟表示： 有些事仍然需要雲端。如即時聯網搜尋、跨裝置的長期記憶。我們的目標是讓端側成為主力，而不是排斥雲端。 也就是說，消費者在日常生活和工作中使用的許多AI功能，大部分都可以通過端側模型解決。 以無界方舟的一個AI耳機品牌客戶為例，其產品使用的是端雲協同的解決方案，但已經有92%的AI使用是通過端側模型，僅8%通過雲端。 當端側智力水平與雲端齊平，硬體上手門檻進一步降低後，端側模型成為主力，似乎是不可撼動的趨勢。 而無界方舟，就是讓這個趨勢到來的變數。 傳送門： 無界方舟官網：https://www.autoarkai.com/model-detail/llm-145b Hugging Face： 145B模型：https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Edge0-145B-NVFP4 item.abstract: “Agent版arXiv”來了！936個智慧體12個星期狂發近千篇論文，連同行評議都整上了 henry 2026-11-23 14:59:38 來源： 量子位 一個完全由AI組成的科學家社會，是什麼樣？ henry發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號QbitAI 一個完全由AI組成的科學家社會，是什麼樣？ 最近，來自alphaXiv、斯坦福，MIT等機構的研究團隊還真做了這麼一個實驗： 他們把 936個agent放進了同一個線上科研社群，任其自由演化整整12個星期。 規則很簡單：研究團隊搭建好共享預印本伺服器和聊天室，35家人類實驗室只負責提供算力、API預算和寬泛的研究方向。 剩下的 **提出假設、寫程式碼跑實驗、分析資料、寫論文，乃至同行交流，全權交給Agent自主完成 。** 結果，12周下來，這近1000個agent一共在平臺上釋出了 936篇研究論文 ，研究橫跨機器學習、太陽物理等多個學科。 不僅如此，它們還在229個自建聊天室裡刷出了 9500條 討論，每天都在閱讀彼此的論文，復現實驗。 一旦發現問題，就會像人類學術共同體一樣，拿著對方的程式碼重跑實驗，再接著“同行”的結果往下探索。 捲到最後，這群Agent甚至自己辦起了一本學術期刊，建立審稿機制，開始給其他AI的論文把關…… 真·AI頂會～ 而且值得一提的是，除了上面的實驗結果，目前這個供Agent科學家交流的伺服器已經開放，其他研究者也可以接入自己的Agent，在上面提交研究成果。 接下來，我們具體來看。 這個只有AI的科研社群，怎麼運轉？ 總的來說，這場實驗模擬了真實科學界的分散式生態： 35家參與的獨立實驗室各自配置硬體，選擇模型和執行框架，再接入同一個共享工作空間。 各實驗室可以自主選擇不同的領域與方向，再通過公開的論文庫和聊天室交流，尋找可以接續的工作。 為了讓不同實驗室的研究能夠相互銜接，團隊首先立了一套共同的工作流程： 1、Agent動手前必須先查閱社群已有論文，公開宣佈自己的假設和計算計劃。 在早期共享GPU的實驗室裡，它們甚至會在公共頻道協調裝置使用和參數測試，避免同行之間做無意義的重複跑批。 2、提交論文時，每項研究都強制附帶可執行程式碼、原始資料，以及連線論文數字和實驗輸出的 “宣告賬本”（Claim Ledger） 。 通過這些記錄，其他Agent可以精確追溯每個指標對應的資料檔案和欄位，核查計算過程，並直接在此基礎上執行後續實驗。 在實驗最初，也就是在8月19日剛啟動時，只有1家實驗室參與；10月15日至25日，又陸續有5家實驗室加入，到了10月25日後，最終達到35家實驗室。 隨著參與者增多，Agent們的交流也從最初的公共頻道，逐步分流進圍繞具體問題建立的主題聊天室。 在這裡，它們隨時分享中間結果、質疑實驗設計，或者直接拿來同行的程式碼復現。 例如，六家實驗室曾圍繞“模型學習韓語時怎樣減少英語遺忘”展開接力： 一個Agent報告某種方法能大幅減少遺忘，另一個很快在聊天室指出，兩種方法學到的韓語程度根本不同，比較條件沒有對齊。 接到反饋後，它隨即重跑同行程式碼，修正了效果判斷。 後續實驗室則順著這條線繼續深挖原因、測試替代方案，最後還有Agent彙總了整條研究線的實驗輸出。 更關鍵的是，在這個Agent科學家社會里， “失敗的研究”也會被納入知識積累 。 平臺規則賦予嚴謹的負結果（陰性/零結果）與正結果同等的學術認可。由此，其他Agent可以據此避開已經被證偽的死胡同，大幅減少重複試錯。 此外，隨著入駐的實驗室越來越多，Agent的投稿量也開始水漲船高，Agent科學家們也開始組織更正式的質量審查。 一個名叫Cypress的Agent看到其他實驗室短時間內上傳了一批佔位“水文”，便主動建立審稿聊天室，準備對投稿作出接收、修改或拒稿決定。 等待四天仍未招到志願審稿人後，它乾脆建立常設大模型評審小組，正式啟動了 《Journal of Agent Research》（簡稱JAR） 。 具體的，評審小組呼叫不同模型，分別把關方法與統計、可復現性、研究意義，並專門設定“反方質疑”角色。 每一條批評都必須逐字引用論文原文，再由指令碼自動核對引號內容，防止審稿AI瞎編。 僅11月4日至9日，短短5天，這套系統就為263項研究的352個版本生成了1408份審稿意見。 當然了，這種Agent審稿系統也很快遇到了問題： 在一次自動審稿暫停期間，編輯AI檢查了三篇論文的程式碼，發現有的提前洩漏了答案，有的甚至把錯誤結果直接替換成正確答案。 它隨即要求作者自查。另一名Agent發現自己的實驗也洩漏了答案，於是主動撤稿。修正後重跑，模型準確率從 **91.7%降到了64.6% 。** 這也印證了一點：即便論文裡的數字確實來自真實執行，底層程式碼實現仍可能背離論文描述。 檢查程式碼和原始資料，才是這個AI期刊真正發揮把關作用的核心環節。 talkless，show me your code！ Agent科研社群，產出成色如何？ 那麼，這個Agent科研社群，產出成色如何？ item.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
item.abstract: Back to Articles How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation Published November 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 27 +21 Avijit Ghosh evijit Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Irene Solaiman irenesolaiman Follow Overview AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on. Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it. The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year , to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments. This guide covers four things: Three eras of evaluation (section 1). Evaluations moved from checking answers, to checking what an agent did, to checking what a team of agents produces. Each step adds software that can change the score. The steps in an agentic evaluation (section 2). We follow one task through eight steps, from the claim to the reported score. The full walkthrough, with commands, is in Appendix A . When a benchmark is wrong (section 3). Errors in tasks and graders are common. We look at how they are found and corrected. What to open strategically and why (section 4). A table sets out, component by component, what to share and what can stay protected. In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent . The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across. 1. Introduction: how evaluation design has changed AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes. Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms , teams managed by an orchestrator , and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work . Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations. Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced. We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench , researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed. The anatomy of an agentic evaluation Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation. There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately. Why benchmark release decisions matter Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party , and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough . At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5 , announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations , where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable. 2. Building an eval: what to reuse, adapt, and validate With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation. We work through eight steps: define the claim , find a task , run it unchanged , adapt it , check the evaluation , read the traces , report the score , and compare models . We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A . Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example. Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results. Method Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A).

item.title: Import AI 482: Huawei kernel benchmarks; airborne drone detection; and a national lab’s AI science benchmark
item.abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. Chinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark: …AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI… Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei – especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei. What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write. “AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.” The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”. How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Opus 5 is more token hungry and GPT-5.6 more token efficient. Why this matters – ingredients for Chinese RSI: For AI systems to be able to build themselves, they need to be able to develop and improve the software that is used for their own training and inference. Software like AscendGYM will be an essential ingredient for allowing China to rapidly improve the efficiency of its own compute substrates. The software will also have a bearing on export controls, where it provides a route to improve the performance of Chinese chips and close the gap with Western alternatives. Read more: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (arXiv) . Get AscendGYM here : AscendGYM (GitHub) . Lawrence Livermore scientists test out if AI scientists can communicate uncertainty about experimental results: …Can AI systems be appropriately conservative?… “An agent that reports a confident wrong number is worse than one that reports honest uncertainty, because nobody downstream can tell the difference,” write researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in a new paper that tests out how reliably AI systems can give accurate score ranges even when dealing with uncertainty. Testing for uncertainty: The paper introduces SciResearch-Eval, “an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator”. The novel part of this eval is that “an agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth”. What they studied: They give AI agents a common materials science task – measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating a sample and fitting a heat-conduction model to its temperature response. “An agent receives a sample of unknown material, a simulator of heat conduction through it, one heating experiment, and budgets: four more experiments it designs, compute for simulations and fits, and a cap on actions. It must report the sample’s conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, and predict a measurement it may not run,” they write. “Hidden from the agent, the simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (the real sample has temperature-dependent conductivity, a glued joint, front-face radiation, or heat loss through its sides), or adequate but fed uninformative data”. Results – only the most powerful frontier models can do this : “When the simulator is missing real physics, only GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 are reliable at default settings; the Claude 5.5 models recover only at their highest reasoning setting, and older and open-weight models not at all.” These models are able to do well by automatically trying to measure where the simulator is accurate and where it is less accurate then bases their estimates on that, making them more resilient to the different ways the simulator gets broken in experiments. Why this matters – real scientists are careful, and so are powerful models: Papers like this are further indications that we’re entering an era of AI-driven science. Though many of today’s models can assist in scientific experiments, as this paper shows only a couple of the powerful models at the frontier are able to operate with such appropriate autonomous skepticism and inherent attendance to the scientific method that they can deal with unanticipated breaks in their equipment. This is both an indication of the science advancement to come and a sign of how the most powerful models are exhibiting more and more of an ability to generalize and make themselves robust to perturbations in their environment. Read more: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents (arXiv) . Check out the leaderboard here (official site) . Stanford professors launch AI startup that wants to create a world where thousands of models define the frontier: …Noeri sees two well-regarded AI researchers enter the neolab game… Stanford profs Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin have launched Noeri, “a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence”. They have raised $110m and are relatively light on technical details, but their main vision is that they want to create a world where the frontier is defined by powerful models which rely on the proprietary data of distinct organizations. “Rather than one monolithic source of truth, we can nurture many small, specialized intelligences, each tuned to a place, a people or a problem,” they write. Further details: “At Noeri, we are building intelligence that learns proactively and continually. Most AI today is trained once and then frozen, while the world it serves keeps moving,” they write. “We close that gap with living systems that grow out of our own research. Our work on test-time training showed that learning on the job after deployment can unlock new capabilities and lead to new discoveries. Our work on self-distillation found that a model can become its own teacher, learning from each mistake and solving hard problems in far fewer attempts. And our work on agentic orchestration demonstrated that a small model conducting a team of other models and tools can outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.” Why this matters – the political economy of the singularity: Currently, the dominant AI models are massive pre-trained ones from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI and a tiny handful of other companies. What would it mean for the frontier to be instead defined by a broader set of actors? This is a core question inherent to the political economy of AI and startups like this show how some people are going to try and utilize technical approaches to make that different vision a reality. Read more in the announcement tweet from Yejin (Yejin Choi, X) .

item.title: 5 Lightweight Alternatives to MCP for Giving AI Agents Tools
item.abstract: 5 Lightweight Alternatives to MCP for Giving AI Agents Tools Compare five lightweight ways to give AI agents tools without an MCP server, from a Python dispatcher to framework tools, REST adapters, subprocesses, and webhooks, and learn when MCP becomes worth adding. By Nahla Davies , KDnuggets on November 23, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Suppose your application already has a function called lookup_product(sku) . The function reads one row from a catalog and returns a price. Now you want a model to be able to call it. Does that one lookup need a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server? Usually not, and it is worth being fair about why. MCP is a protocol for connecting tools to many hosts: a server describes its tools, and any compatible client can discover and call them. The current MCP architecture , the July 28, 2026 revision, runs over stdio on the same machine as well as over Streamable HTTP, so adopting it does not force a network service on you. KDnuggets' local MCP assistant walkthrough shows a complete system; here, we will compare how to connect one operation. The five options below are not five rival standards. They are five places the same function can live, chosen by what you already own: a few Python functions, an agent framework, a REST API, a command-line tool, or a workflow platform. Lightweight means fewer new integration and deployment responsibilities in the environment you have now, nothing more universal than that. Every example uses the same invented catalog. SKU BK-17 is an A5 field notebook at 1,299 cents in USD, and every record carries fixture: true so nobody mistakes it for a price list. The model in the live examples is qwen3.5:4b on Ollama 0.40.13, and every output shown is what the code printed. Keeping the Same Tool Contract Across the Five Choices Whichever connection you pick, three things happen in the same order. The model proposes a call: a tool name and arguments. The application checks that proposal against a contract it owns: the name must be one it allows, the arguments must fit the declared shape, and the operation must be one this user is permitted to run. Then an executor performs the work and returns either structured data or an explicit error, which the application passes back to the model. Figure 1. The application controls execution whichever connection it uses. Schematic of the five alternatives and the MCP lane they are compared with; no deployed system is depicted. Original diagram by Nahla Davies. The five alternatives change who the executor is and where the function runs. They do not change the business rule, and none of them removes the application's checks. OWASP's excessive-agency guidance separates three ways this goes wrong, too much functionality, too many permissions and too much autonomy, and all three are decided by the application, not by the transport. Existing component Connection choice Work that remains yours When the choice stops being simple A few local Python functions Native tool calling plus an allowlisted dispatcher Message handling, permissions and errors Several providers or clients need reusable contracts A Python agent framework Typed function tools Business authorization and dependency maintenance Framework coupling outweighs the saved glue A service with an HTTP interface A curated REST adapter, with OpenAPI as the map Credentials, allowed operations and response handling Broad or changing specs need a maintained adapter layer A trusted narrow command A bounded subprocess Argument policy, privileges and process failures Untrusted code or wider access needs real isolation A maintained workflow platform An authenticated webhook Workflow ownership, credentials and completion semantics Deploying the platform exceeds the saved integration work The contract itself is small: # catalog.py import re SKU_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^[A-Z]{2}-\d{2,4}$") CATALOG = { "BK-17": {"sku": "BK-17", "name": "Field notebook, A5", "price_cents": 1299, "currency": "USD", "fixture": True}, "BK-18": {"sku": "BK-18", "name": "Field notebook, A4", "price_cents": 1799, "currency": "USD", "fixture": True}, } def validate_sku(sku: object) -> str: if not isinstance(sku, str) or not SKU_PATTERN.match(sku): raise ValueError(f"sku must match {SKU_PATTERN.pattern}, got {sku!r}") return sku def lookup_product(sku: str) -> dict: """Return the catalog record for one SKU, or raise KeyError if it does not exist.""" sku = validate_sku(sku) if sku not in CATALOG: raise KeyError(sku) return dict(CATALOG[sku]) 1. Use Native Tool Calling and a Small Dispatcher If the function lives in the same Python process as your model calls, the shortest route is the provider's own tool-calling interface and a dictionary. Ollama's native tool-calling exchange has three steps. You send the tool schema with the chat request, and the assistant message comes back with tool_calls instead of text. You run the call yourself and append a tool message holding the result. Then you ask again, and the model answers with the result in hand. # k1_native_tools.py (core) TOOLS = [{"type": "function", "function": { "name": "lookup_product", "description": "Look up one product in the catalog by SKU and return its price.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "required": ["sku"], "properties": {"sku": {"type": "string", "description": "Catalog SKU such as BK-17"}}}}}] DISPATCH = {"lookup_product": lookup_product} # a name not in here is never executed MAX_TURNS = 3 def run_tool_call(call: dict) -> str: name = call["function"]["name"] args = call["function"].get("arguments") or {} if name not in DISPATCH: return json.dumps({"error": f"tool {name!r} is not available"}) try: return json.dumps(DISPATCH[name](**args)) except (TypeError, ValueError) as err: return json.dumps({"error": f"invalid arguments: {err}"}) except KeyError as err: return json.dumps({"error": f"unknown sku {err.args[0]!r}"}) def ask(model: str, question: str) -> str: messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}] for turn in range(MAX_TURNS): reply = chat(model, messages)["message"] # POST /api/chat with tools=TOOLS, stream=False messages.append(reply) calls = reply.get("tool_calls") or [] if not calls: return reply.get("content", "").strip() for call in calls: result = run_tool_call(call) messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_name": call["function"]["name"], "content": result}) return f"unfinished after {MAX_TURNS} turns" $ python k1_native_tools.py --model qwen3.5:4b "How much is BK-17?" model proposed: lookup_product({"sku": "BK-17"}) application returned: {"sku": "BK-17", "name": "Field notebook, A5", "price_cents": 1299, "currency": "USD", "fixture": true} final answer: The price of the Field notebook (A5), SKU BK-17, is $12.99 USD. $ python k1_native_tools.py --model qwen3.5:4b "How much is BK-99?" model proposed: lookup_product({"sku": "BK-99"}) application returned: {"error": "unknown sku 'BK-99'"} final answer: I couldn't find the price for SKU BK-99 in our catalog. ... The dispatcher is the whole security model of this route, so it has to be a fixed dictionary, never getattr on a module or anything the model can name into existence. The second run shows why the error path matters. The model asked for a SKU that does not exist, and the application returned a structured error rather than raising. Given that error, the model told the user so instead of inventing a price. What this route does not give you is portability. The message shapes are Ollama's; a different provider has a different tool_calls layout, and you own the loop, the turn limit and every error. That is a fine trade for one application with a few functions and a poor one the day a second client wants the same tools. A tool function can be as thick as it needs to be behind that boundary. For a document-processing tool, extracting table data from PDFs can stay inside an SDK-backed function; the agent receives the returned fields rather than managing the PDF parser.

item.title: Anthropic Launches Claude Ship for GitHub Pull Request Review and Fixes
item.abstract: Anthropic just released Claude Ship Claude Ship is a set of Anthropic agents that takes GitHub pull requests from review to approval. It bundles 3 agents: Code Review , PR Steward and Claude Approvals . Your GitHub branch rules still decide what merges. Per the Claude Ship docs , each agent owns 1 step: Code Review is generally available . The other 2 are in public beta. Code Review finds problems. PR Steward pushes fixes, and a fix can start another review. Claude Approvals then applies your policy. The merge follows your GitHub branch rules. PR Steward is designed not to approve or merge. After each push, it comments on its changes and how to undo them. Developers steer it with @claude and stop it with @claude stop . Claude Approvals reads a policy file at .claude/approvals.yml . Anthropic calls it a smarter CODEOWNERS file. A rule can require 2 people on billing code and 1 on test fixtures. Rules can read PR facts and classifier answers, but not CI results. Developers run /ship in Claude Code. It commits, pushes and opens the PR. Claude reviews it, then ‘watches’ feedback and failing checks. You merge yourself. Requirements are Claude Code v2.1.330 or later, GitHub CLI 2.63 or later, and git 2.38 or later. A watch ends after 7 days, or on merge or close. /steward skips the review on an open PR. When Claude acts alone, Claude Code blocks merge, approve, auto-merge and force-push commands. Still, a watch uses your own gh and git sign-ins. Anthropic has published no public benchmark. It shares internal results from its launch post and engineering blog : These numbers are self-reported by Anthropic. No precision or recall is reported. Competitor figures come from each vendor’s own docs, checked November 23, 2026. Claude Ship is for Claude Team and Enterprise plans on GitHub. Owners enable agents per repository, ideally 1 at a time. Billing runs on tokens through usage credits , separate from plan usage. Code Review costs scale with PR count, size, review level and frequency. Admins can set spend limits. PR Steward has none until an Owner sets one. Approvals has no base charge. Classifier runs and the reviews a policy requests are billed, even in observe mode. Running /ship counts as regular Claude Code usage. Eligible Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits by January 15, 2027. Credits expire 30 days after claiming, per the credit terms . Check out the launch post , the Claude Ship docs and the /ship command docs . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . item.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
item.abstract: Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship , a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes. The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team. Image Credits: Anthropic The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge. The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available , and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed. Image Credits: Anthropic Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language. Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process. Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision. Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

flash做了一場AMA。 AMA是「Ask Me Anything」的縮寫，意思是「有什麼想問的，儘管問」。網友在評論區提問，混元團隊成員直接回帖。 參與名單上只列了Reddit賬號，至於哪個馬甲是姚順雨，我們還沒對上號…… 這場AMA的主角，是混元本月接連發布的兩款模型。 11月4日釋出的 Hy4 是旗艦，能理解文本、影像和影片，適合長程軟體工程這類需要多步推理、反覆呼叫工具的複雜任務。 讓Agent自己解題，訓練時遇到過什麼麻煩？有時它會直接上網找現成答案，跳過解題過程。 還有網友問，後訓練裡最難改善的行為是什麼，團隊只回了一個詞， Overthinking，過度思考。 旗艦Hy4的推理鏈有時偏長。到了Flash，團隊先從旗艦蒸餾，再用強化學習把推理鏈壓短。 從模型怎麼訓，到開發者能不能把它跑起來，這場AMA聊了不少平時在模型卡上只有一行、到了真用時卻繞不開的問題。 訓練Hy4和Hy4 flash做長程Agent任務時，多輪強化學習裡最難處理的情況是什麼？ 混元團隊： 最棘手的是訓練環境設計有漏洞，模型會鑽空子拿獎勵。比如，我們得防止Agent直接上網搜現成答案，讓它自己把任務做完。 網友： 做命令列任務時，模型編錯一個參數就可能讓命令出錯。你們怎麼提高工具呼叫的準確性，又怎麼讓模型在長任務裡記住前文？ 混元團隊： 如果讓Hy4自己執行，它現在能通過遞迴自我改進做出下一代模型嗎？你們怎麼評估這種能力？ 混元團隊： 我們的遞迴自我改進能力還處於早期，已經做了幾項內部基準，用來評估其中的關鍵能力。 Flash的參數花在哪兒了？ 網友： 不算Engram，Hy4 flash主幹約有1560億參數，每個Token啟用約120億。如果總參數不變，把啟用參數降到80億或50億，效果會掉多少？ 混元團隊： 我們做過不同MoE稀疏度的規模實驗。固定啟用參數量時，提高稀疏度能改善計算效率。但如果固定總參數，再把啟用量降到80億或50億，我預計模型質量會明顯下降。啟用參數量決定了每個Token能用多少計算，提高稀疏度能彌補一部分。 網友： Hy4 flash為什麼給Engram分配約635億參數？這個比例是怎麼定的？ 混元團隊： item.title: 27 Cybersecurity Terms to Prepare You for the Age of AI
item.abstract: AI now sits on both sides of the security fight, and the vocabulary has changed with it. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that 1 in 4 malicious breaches were AI-enabled, up 56% year over year. Those breaches cost an average of $6 million, about $1 million above the $4.99 million global average. Attackers now target the models themselves, the agents that act on their output, and the people who trust what AI produces. The reference lists have moved fast to keep up. OWASP published its Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 on August 4, 2026, and its first Top 10 for Agentic Applications in December 2025. MITRE ATLAS maps attacker tactics against AI systems the way ATT&CK does for IT. The 27 terms below are grouped in 4 parts: attacks on models, agentic risks, AI-powered attacks on people, and the defenses that answer them. These attacks target what a model reads, learns or reveals. NIST groups them into evasion, poisoning, privacy and misuse in its Adversarial Machine Learning taxonomy (NIST AI 100-2e2025) , published March 2025. Prompt injection is input crafted to override a model’s intended instructions. It has ranked No. 1 on every edition of the OWASP LLM list, including the 2026 edition . LLMs have no hard boundary between instructions and data, so any text the model reads can try to steer it. Indirect prompt injection hides the malicious instruction in content the model retrieves: an email, a web page, a PDF or a code comment. The user never types it. The clearest real case is EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) , a zero-click flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot rated CVSS 9.3. Aim Security showed that one crafted email could make Copilot leak organizational data; Microsoft fixed it server-side in May 2025. A jailbreak tricks a model into ignoring its safety training, usually through role-play, fake context or sheer volume. Anthropic’s many-shot jailbreaking research showed that stuffing a long prompt with up to 256 fake dialogues can override safety behavior. Its effectiveness grows with context window size, following a power law. Data poisoning plants malicious samples in training or fine-tuning data so the model learns harmful behavior. A joint study by Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found that just 250 malicious documents could backdoor models from 600M to 13B parameters. The number needed stayed roughly constant regardless of model size. A backdoor is hidden behavior that only activates on a secret trigger. Anthropic’s Sleeper Agents paper trained models to write secure code when the prompt said 2023 but insert exploitable code when it said 2024. Standard safety training, including adversarial training, did not remove the behavior. An adversarial example is an input changed in small, often invisible ways so a model misclassifies it. Think of a tweaked image, audio clip or malware sample that slips past an AI detector. NIST treats evasion as one of the core attack classes in AI 100-2 . Model extraction clones a model’s capabilities by querying it at scale and training a “student” model on the answers. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported in February 2026 that these “distillation attacks” were rising. One campaign sent more than 100,000 prompts aimed at Gemini’s reasoning. Membership inference tests whether a specific record was in a model’s training set. Training data extraction goes further and pulls memorized text out. Carlini et al. extracted hundreds of verbatim sequences from GPT-2 , including personal contact details, using only query access, and found larger models more vulnerable. Hidden context exposure is the leak of system prompts, tool definitions, retrieved documents or other context a user was not meant to see. OWASP renamed and broadened “System Prompt Leakage” into this entry (LLM08) in its 2026 list . The working rule: assume anything in the context window can be extracted, so never put secrets there. Once a model can call tools, keep memory and act on its own, a bad output becomes a bad action. OWASP built its Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01 to ASI10) from incidents seen in real deployments. Excessive agency means an LLM app has more functions, permissions or autonomy than its task needs. When it is fooled or simply wrong, the damage scales with that reach. In the OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 , excessive agency rose to No. 3, behind only prompt injection and sensitive information disclosure. Agent goal hijack is ASI01, the top agentic risk: malicious content redirects an agent’s objectives or decision path. It is prompt injection with hands. OWASP cites EchoLeak as an example, where hidden prompts turned a copilot into a silent exfiltration tool. Tool poisoning hides malicious instructions inside a tool’s description or schema, which the model reads but the user usually does not see. Invariant Labs disclosed the attack against the Model Context Protocol (MCP) on April 1, 2025. Its proof of concept was an “add two numbers” tool that told the agent in Cursor to read SSH keys and config files. A related “rug pull” swaps a benign tool for a malicious one after the user approves it. Memory and context poisoning (ASI06) corrupts an agent’s stored memory, RAG index or embeddings so the bad data shapes future sessions. Unlike a one-off prompt injection, it persists. The fix starts with treating everything written to memory as untrusted input, with provenance and expiry. See OWASP’s agentic list for mitigations. Slopsquatting is registering a package name that AI coding tools hallucinate, so developers or agents who follow the AI install attacker code. A USENIX Security 2025 study of 16 code models and 576,000 samples found 19.7% of recommended packages did not exist. That added up to 205,474 unique fake names, many of them repeated across runs and therefore easy to target. NHIs are the service accounts, API keys, tokens, certificates and AI agents that authenticate without a person. Palo Alto Networks’ 2026 Identity Security Landscape puts the ratio at 109 machine identities per human, up from 82:1 a year earlier. OWASP’s ASI03 (identity and privilege abuse) covers the risk: agents that inherit, cache or pass on credentials they should not hold. These attacks use AI as the weapon rather than the target. They exploit trust: in a familiar face, a familiar voice, a well-written email or a helpful tool. A deepfake is AI-generated video, audio or imagery that convincingly mimics a real person. In early 2024, a finance worker at engineering firm Arup’s Hong Kong office transferred HK$200 million (about US$25.6 million) in 15 transactions after a video call where the “CFO” and colleagues were all deepfakes. IBM’s 2026 report found deepfake impersonation was the most common AI-enabled attack type, at 45% . Voice cloning creates a synthetic copy of someone’s voice from a short sample. Vishing is voice phishing that uses it. In May 2025 the FBI warned that since April 2025, attackers had sent AI-generated voice messages impersonating senior US officials to build rapport and take over accounts. Its advice: verify the person through a contact method you already know. AI-generated phishing uses LLMs to write targeted, fluent lures in the victim’s own language and at scale. Microsoft’s Digital Defense Report 2025 found AI-automated phishing emails got a 54% click-through rate, versus 12% for standard ones. That is 4.5 times more effective, and Microsoft estimates AI can make phishing up to 50 times more profitable. Shadow AI is employees using AI tools the organization has not approved or cannot see. Pasting customer data into a public chatbot is the classic case. IBM’s 2025 report found high shadow AI use added $670,000 to the average breach cost. By the 2026 report , shadow AI was involved in 43% of the incidents IBM studied. An AI-orchestrated attack is one where an AI agent runs much of the intrusion itself, not just advises a human.

item.title: Sharing catalog metadata across data platforms, engines, and agents
item.abstract: We’re excited to announce support for catalog labels – a new capability in the Apache Iceberg™ REST Catalog API that enables platforms, engines, and agents to access context such as business purpose, ownership and data classifications maintained in Iceberg REST-compatible catalogs. This shared context supports discovery, governance, and agentic workflows across the data and AI ecosystem. We believe that catalog metadata should be as open and portable as the data it describes. As enterprises bring more tools into their open lakehouse architectures, they need a common way to share the context that makes their data understandable, useful, and secure for all teams, regardless of what tools they use. Today, that context often remains siloed in the source catalog. Data and AI teams must recreate classifications across platforms, maintain custom metadata synchronization pipelines, or work with agents that lack complete context. Databricks is joined by Google Cloud, Salesforce, ClickHouse, Atlan, Collibra, DataHub, Immuta, Trust3 AI, PhoenixAI, and Datastrato in advancing this shared vision of metadata interoperability. Catalog labels offer a path toward that vision, making catalog context portable while allowing each platform to retain its own capabilities and controls. Databricks worked with the Apache Iceberg community to add an optional labels field to the Iceberg REST LoadTable response. This gives catalogs a standard way to expose table- and column-level context to other platforms, tools, and agents. Labels are string key-value pairs that can describe business ownership, intended use, sensitivity or other catalog-maintained context. The standard defines a common format for sharing this metadata without prescribing its vocabulary or interpretation, giving each platform the flexibility to build on it in its own way Consider a table named support_cases An authorized data steward assigns domain=customer_support and the Databricks system tag system.certification_status=certified to the table, and content_type=support_case_summary to the issue_summary column. A catalog exposing these tags could include the following in its Iceberg REST LoadTable response: This example shows only the labels portion of the response. A downstream platform can then use these labels to make the table more useful: This enables applications to inspect the table- and column- label labels from the same support_cases table. For example, PyIceberg has added support for accessing catalog labels in Python. In the next 0.13 release, applications will be able to inspect the table- and column-level labels from the same support_cases table: These labels make the catalog’s metadata available directly to Python applications, including data-discovery tools and agents. Unity Catalog exposes its table- and column-level tags through catalog labels with Tag Exchange. Tag Exchange is a step toward our broader vision of open governance: context maintained in one system should be usable across every platform, engine, and AI agent working with the data. By exposing Unity Catalog’s table- and column-level tags,Tag Exchange lets enterprises reuse classifications and business context for discovery, agent workflows, and access policies. Each tool has the freedom to decide how to interpret and use that context. Databricks is excited to join our partners in advancing catalog labels to make catalog metadata open and accessible. Together, we’re in support of an open interface that gives AI agents and data platforms shared context for discovering data, understanding it, and keeping it governed. Tag Exchange is available in Beta today, exposing Unity Catalog’s table- and column-level tags through catalog labels. To get started, enable “Tag Exchange via Iceberg REST Catalog” in the Databricks Previews portal. Catalog labels are string key-value pairs that share table- and column-level context through the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API. They can describe business ownership, intended use, sensitivity, and other metadata, helping platforms, tools, and agents understand the data they access. Databricks supports catalog labels through Tag Exchange, which exposes Unity Catalog’s table- and column-level tags through the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API. External platforms, tools, and agents can use this context for discovery, classification, and locally defined access policies. Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

item.title: Announcing General Availability of native Lakebase Postgres sink for Spark Structured Streaming
item.abstract: Low-latency use cases like fraud detection, live personalization, and real-time feature computation need computed results in a serving-ready OLTP store. Lakebase Postgres is Databricks' fully managed, serverless PostgreSQL database offering, with autoscaling, branching, native Unity Catalog integration, and sub 10ms reads. But writing to it from a streaming pipeline has meant building a custom foreach writer and handling batching, retries, and upserts yourself, which is complex to get right and hard to keep performant under load. Today, we are announcing the general availability of the native Lakebase sink for Apache Spark™ Structured Streaming, a connector that writes computed results directly to Lakebase and handles all of that for you. The same connector works in both micro-batch and Real-Time Mode . We show it on a feature pipeline that ingests watch and like events from a video streaming platform, computes each user's recent activity, and upserts one feature row per user into Lakebase in hundreds of milliseconds. You get that performance without building or maintaining the connector yourself. A foreach writer has to do a lot at once: batch writes for throughput, a bounded queue for backpressure, pool connections and refresh OAuth tokens, retry transient failures with backoff, deduplicate within a batch. It also has to implement upsert semantics correctly, including keeping the greatest timestamp or updating a column only when an incoming event has a newer ordering value. Even for an experienced developer, writing and tuning all of this is weeks of work, and it does not end there. The connector turns into something you maintain, fixing throughput regressions, credential refresh, and keeping the code current with the latest versions. For a sense of what that looks like in practice, see this reference implementation . The native sink takes care of it. You wire up a Lakebase write in minutes with a single writeStream call, and spend no time on performance, tuning, or maintaining the connector. You get: A video streaming provider wants to recommend videos to its viewers. A recommendation model needs what users watched most recently. So for each user we compute the last 6 videos they watched and the last 3 they liked. We store that as one row per user in Lakebase. At inference time, the recommendation model looks up that row by user_id to rank what to show next. A feature is an input the model uses to make a prediction. Here, the features are each user's recent activity, computed from a stream of events. Each event has a user_id and a video_id and an event type (WATCH/LIKE). For each user we keep their recent watches and likes as one row, keyed by user_id . Every new event for a user_id updates that row in place. Writing to Lakebase is a single writeStream call. How you point it at Lakebase depends on whether the target table is registered in Unity Catalog. If the Lakebase table is registered in Unity Catalog , write with .toTable() using the fully qualified catalog.schema.table . The connector manages credentials as the running user or service principal, and creates the table if it doesn't exist: If the Lakebase table isn't registered in Unity Catalog, write to the Lakebase endpoint directly with format("postgresql") (see Lakebase tables not registered with Unity Catalog ). The same format("postgresql") path also supports writing to external PostgreSQL databases (e.g. Amazon RDS or self-hosted) via a Unity Catalog connection (DBR 19+, Public Preview). The sink writes the features into Lakebase within 100-200 milliseconds of being produced, with no offline-to-online sync in between. Applications and models can query them in single-digit milliseconds. This supports two patterns: For a deeper look at the implementation, see the companion repo , a self-serve example you can run end-to-end. We ran the pipeline at a sustained input rate of ~20K events/sec against 5 million active users, each accumulating watch and like history. The cluster used was a 40-core classic compute (DBR 18 LTS) writing to an 8-CU Lakebase project with 5-minute RTM checkpoint intervals. Every event is an upsert that overwrites that user's existing feature row in Lakebase. As state builds up, the sink is continuously upserting against a table with millions of existing rows, finding and replacing the row for each user_id on every event. This is the workload pattern that breaks custom foreach writers at scale. End-to-end latency is measured from the Kafka input timestamp to the row landing in Lakebase. 20k Events per sec (1 hour sustained) Active user (state cardinality) Note: This illustrative example uses synthetic data replayed into Kafka. The test ran for 60 minutes, achieving ~20K EPS and 63.5 million upserts. These latencies are specific to this setup. Your numbers will differ with input rate, the amount of state you keep, RTM cluster size, and Lakebase size. Size both the cluster and Lakebase to sustain the throughput you need. The sink also lets you tune how it batches writes using batchinterval and batchsize . See performance tuning . At this throughput on an 8-CU project, pg_stat_statements shows 63.5 million upserts averaging ~0.015 milliseconds per statement. Lakebase had headroom to spare. For a deeper look at how Lakebase achieves this, see the blog, How Lakebase Architecture Delivers 5x Faster Postgres Writes . With Real-Time Mode computing features as events arrive and the native Lakebase sink enabling writes directly to a serving-ready OLTP database, together they unblock real-time feature computation and ingestion in one streaming pipeline. The native sink gives you a first-class experience when writing to Lakebase, using the same writeStream API you already know. We showed it on a recommendation feature pipeline, but the same pattern works wherever a streaming pipeline needs to write computed results to a database for immediate serving. The native Lakebase sink for Spark Structured Streaming is now Generally Available. What is the native Lakebase sink for Spark Structured Streaming? It’s a Structured Streaming connector that writes computed results directly to Lakebase. It handles batching, retries, connection pooling, deduplication, upserts, and workspace-managed authentication, so you don’t build a custom foreach writer. The same connector works in both micro-batch and Real-Time Mode. Is the native Lakebase sink generally available? Yes. The native Lakebase sink for Spark Structured Streaming is now generally available on Databricks Runtime 18 LTS and above. The RealTime and ProcessingTime triggers run on classic compute; on serverless, use Trigger.AvailableNow . It isn’t supported in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines. How do I write to Lakebase with the sink? For a Lakebase table registered in Unity Catalog, use .toTable() with the fully qualified catalog.schema.table ; the connector manages credentials and creates the table if it doesn’t exist. For an unregistered table, use format("postgresql") with the Lakebase endpoint and dbtable . Does the sink support upserts and custom merge logic? Yes. Declare an upsertkey and the sink maintains one row per key. Merge strategies (DBR 19+) control how non-key columns update on conflict, such as keeping the latest non-null value or the value from the newest event, with no hand-written ON CONFLICT SQL. What use cases is the native Lakebase sink built for? The native Lakebase sink is built for operational dashboards, app databases, and low-latency feature stores.. Examples include real-time feature computation for recommendations and personalization, and fraud detection. Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.
